nodes.name: alpha-maximal clique reduces to maximal clique for alpha=1
nodes.statement: When $\alpha=1$, the above definition reduces to the well understood notion of a maximal clique in a deterministic graph.

nodes.name: Uncertain graph
nodes.statement: An uncertain graph is a probability distribution over a set of deterministic graphs. We deal with undirected simple graphs, i.e. there are no self-loops or multiple edges. An uncertain graph is a triple $\mathcal{G}=(V,E,p)$, where $V$ is a set of vertices, $E \subseteq V \times V$ is a set of (possible) edges, and $p:E \rightarrow(0,1]$ is a function that assigns a probability of existence $p(e)$ to each edge $e \in E$.
nodes.genus: probability distribution over a set of deterministic graphs
differentia: $p:E \rightarrow(0,1]$ is a function that assigns a probability of existence $p(e)$ to each edge $e \in E$
nodes.statement_short: An uncertain graph is a triple (V,E,p) of vertices, possible edges and edge existence probabilities.

nodes.name: Independence of edge existence
nodes.statement: As in prior work on uncertain graphs, we assume that the existence of different edges are mutually independent events.

nodes.name: n and m
nodes.statement: Let $n=|V|$ and $m=|E|$.

nodes.name: Possible graphs of an uncertain graph
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathcal{G}$ is a distribution over $2^m$ deterministic graphs, each of which is a subgraph of the undirected graph $(V,E)$. This set of possible deterministic graphs is called the set of ``possible graphs'' of the uncertain graph $\mathcal{G}$, and is denoted by $D(\mathcal{G})$.

nodes.name: Adjacency in an uncertain graph
nodes.statement: In an uncertain graph $\mathcal{G}=(V,E,p)$, two vertices $u$ and $v$ are said to be adjacent if there exists an edge $\{u,v\}$ in $E$.

nodes.name: Neighborhood
nodes.statement: Let the neighborhood of vertex $u$, denoted $\Gamma(u)$, be the set of all vertices that are adjacent to $u$ in $\mathcal{G}$.

nodes.name: Clique
nodes.statement: A set of vertices $C \subseteq V$ is a clique in a graph $G=(V,E)$, if every pair of vertices in $C$ is connected by an edge in $E$.
differentia: every pair of vertices in $C$ is connected by an edge in $E$
nodes.label: def:CliqueInPossibleGraph

nodes.name: Maximal clique
nodes.statement: A set of vertices $M \subseteq V$ is a maximal clique in a graph $G=(V,E)$, if (1)~$M$ is a clique in $G$ and (2)~There is no vertex $v \in V \setminus M$ such that $M \cup \{v\}$ is a clique in $G$.
differentia: There is no vertex $v \in V \setminus M$ such that $M \cup \{v\}$ is a clique in $G$
also_stated_at: Typically, we are interested in a {\em maximal clique}, which is a clique that is not contained within any other clique.
nodes.label: def:MaxCliqueInPossibleGraph

nodes.name: Clique probability and alpha-clique
nodes.statement: In an uncertain graph $\mathcal{G}$, for a set of vertices $C \subseteq V$, the clique probability of $C$, denoted by $clq(C,\mathcal{G})$, is defined as the probability that in a graph sampled from $\mathcal{G}$, $C$ is a clique. For parameter $0 \le \alpha \le 1$, $C$ is called an $\alpha$-clique if $clq(C,\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: clq(C,G) is the probability that C is a clique in a sample of G; C is an alpha-clique if clq(C,G) >= alpha.

nodes.name: Edge set E_C
nodes.statement: For any set of vertices $C \subseteq V$, let $E_C$ denote the set of edges $\{e=\{u,v\} | e \in E, u,v \in C \mbox{ and } u \neq v\}$, i.e. the set of edges connecting vertices in $C$.

nodes.name: Clique probability as product of edge probabilities
nodes.statement: For any set of vertices $C \subseteq V$ in $\mathcal{G}=(V,E,p)$, such that $C$ is a clique in $G=(V,E)$, $clq(C,\mathcal{G}) = \prod_{\substack{e \in E_C}} p(e)$.
nodes.label: obs:Prod

nodes.name: Proof of Observation 1
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a graph sampled from $\mathcal{G}$. The set $C$ will be a clique in $G$ iff every edge in $E_C$ is present in $G$. Since the events of selecting different edges are independent of each other, the observation follows.
nodes.statement_short: C is a clique iff all edges of E_C appear; independence of edges gives the product.

nodes.name: alpha-maximal clique
nodes.statement: Given an uncertain graph $\mathcal{G}=(V,E,p)$, and a parameter $0 \le \alpha \le 1$, a set $M \subseteq V$ is defined as an $\alpha$-maximal clique if (1)~$M$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$, and (2)~There is no vertex $v \in (V \setminus M)$ such that $M \cup \{v\}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$.
differentia: There is no vertex $v \in (V \setminus M)$ such that $M \cup \{v\}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$
also_stated_at: A set of vertices $U$ in an uncertain graph is an $\alpha$-maximal clique if $U$ is a clique with probability at least $\alpha$, and there does not exist a vertex set $U'$ such that $U \subset U'$ and $U'$ is a clique with probability at least $\alpha$.
nodes.label: def:MaxCliqueUncertainGraph2

nodes.name: Maximal Clique Enumeration in an Uncertain Graph
nodes.statement: The {\bf Maximal Clique Enumeration} problem in an Uncertain Graph $\mathcal{G}$ is to enumerate all vertex sets $M \subseteq V$ such that $M$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique in $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.label: def:MaxCliqueEnumProblem

nodes.name: Proof of Observations 2 and 3
nodes.statement: The following two observations follow directly from Observation~\ref{obs:Prod}.
nodes.statement_short: Both follow directly from the product formula of Observation 1.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of clique probability under subsets
nodes.statement: For any two vertex sets $A,B$ in $\mathcal{G}$, if $B \subset A$ then, $clq(B,\mathcal{G}) \ge clq(A,\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.label: obs:Sub

nodes.name: Edges of an alpha-clique have probability at least alpha
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. Then for all $e \in E_C$ we have $p(e) \geq \alpha$.
nodes.label: obs:Elim

nodes.name: Moon-Moser theorem
nodes.statement: The maximum number of maximal cliques in a deterministic graph on $n$ vertices is known exactly due to a result by Moon and Moser~\cite{MM65}. If $n \mod 3 = 0$, this number is $3^{\frac{n}{3}}$. If $n \mod 3 = 1$, then it is $4 \cdot 3^{\frac{n-4}{3}}$, and if $n \mod 3 = 2$, then it is $2 \cdot 3^{\frac{n-2}{3}}$.
nodes.statement_short: The maximum number of maximal cliques in an n-vertex graph is about 3^{n/3}, with exact forms by n mod 3.

nodes.name: Moon-Moser graphs
nodes.statement: The graphs that have the maximum number of maximal cliques are known as Moon-Moser graphs.

nodes.name: f(n, alpha)
nodes.statement: For $0 < \alpha < 1$, let $f(n,\alpha)$ be the maximum number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques in any uncertain graph with $n$ nodes, without any assumption about the assignments of edge probabilities.

nodes.name: Maximum number of alpha-maximal cliques
nodes.statement: Let $n \ge 2$, and $0 < \alpha < 1$. Then: $f(n,\alpha)$ $=$ $n \choose {\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$
also_stated_at: We show that for any $0 < \alpha < 1$, the maximum number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques possible in an uncertain graph is $n \choose \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$, i.e. there is an uncertain graph on $n$ vertices with $n \choose \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ uncertain maximal cliques and no uncertain graph on $n$ vertices can have more than $n \choose \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ $\alpha$-maximal cliques.
nodes.statement_short: For 0<alpha<1 the maximum number of alpha-maximal cliques on n vertices is the central binomial coefficient.
nodes.label: thm:maximum

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: We can easily verify that the theorem holds for $n=2$. for $n \ge 3$, let $g(n) = {n \choose {\lfloor n/2\rfloor}}$. We show $f(n,\alpha)$ is at least $g(n)$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:maxCliq}, and then show that $f(n,\alpha)$ is no more than $g(n)$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:UpperBound}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the lower-bound construction (Lemma 1) with the upper bound (Lemma 2); n=2 checked directly.

nodes.name: Lower-bound construction for alpha-maximal cliques
nodes.statement: For any $n \ge 3$, and any $\alpha, 0 < \alpha < 1$, there exists an uncertain graph $\mathcal{G} = (V,E,p)$ with $n$ nodes which has $g(n)$ $\alpha$-maximal cliques.
conclusions: there exists an uncertain graph $\mathcal{G} = (V,E,p)$ with $n$ nodes which has $g(n)$ $\alpha$-maximal cliques
nodes.label: lem:maxCliq

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: First, we assume that $n$ is even. Consider $\mathcal{G} = (V,E,p)$, where $E = V \times V$. Let $\mbox{$\kappa = {{n/2} \choose 2}$}$. For each $e \in E$, let $p(e)=q$ where $q^{\kappa}=\alpha$. We have $0 <q <1$ since $0< \alpha <1$. Let $S$ be an arbitrary subset of $V$ such that $|S|=n/2$. We can verify that $S$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique since (1)~the probability that $S$ is a clique is $q^{\kappa}=\alpha$ and (2)~for any set $S^\prime \supsetneq S, S^\prime \subseteq V$, the probability that $S^\prime$ is a clique is at most $q q^{\kappa}=q\alpha <\alpha$. We can also observe that for any subset $S \subseteq V$, $S$ cannot be an $\alpha$-maximal clique if $|S|< n/2$ or $|S|> n/2$. Thus we conclude that a subset $S\subseteq V$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique iff $|S|=n/2$ which implies that the total number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$ is $n \choose {n/2}$. A similar proof applies when $n$ is odd.
nodes.statement_short: Construction: complete graph with uniform edge probability q, q^{C(n/2,2)}=alpha, makes exactly the n/2-subsets alpha-maximal.

nodes.name: Case alpha = 1
nodes.statement: Note that our construction in the Lemma above employs the condition that $n \ge 3$ and $0<\alpha <1$. When $\alpha = 1$, the upper bound is from the result of Moon and Moser for deterministic graphs, and in this case $f(n,\alpha) = 3^{\frac{n}{3}}$ and is smaller than $g(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: The construction needs alpha<1; for alpha=1, Moon-Moser gives f = 3^{n/3} < g(n).

nodes.name: Non-redundant collection of sets
nodes.statement:
A collection of sets $\mathcal{C}$ is said to be non-redundant if for any pair $S_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}$, $S_1 
e S_2$, we have $S_1 
subseteq S_2$ and $S_2 
subseteq S_1$.
differentia:
for any pair $S_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}$, $S_1 
e S_2$, we have $S_1 
subseteq S_2$ and $S_2 
subseteq S_1$
nodes.label: defn:non-redundant

nodes.name: Upper bound g(n) on f(n,alpha)
nodes.statement: $g(n)$ is an upper bound on $f(n,\alpha)$.
nodes.label: lem:UpperBound

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}^{\alpha}(\mathcal{G})$ be the collection of all $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$. Note that by the definition of $\alpha$-maximal cliques, any $\alpha$-maximal clique $S$ in $\mathcal{G}$ can not be a proper subset of any other $\alpha$-maximal clique in $\mathcal{G}$. Thus from Definition~\ref{defn:non-redundant}, for any uncertain graph $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{C}^{\alpha}(\mathcal{G})$ is a non-redundant collection. Hence, it is clear that the largest number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$ should be upper bounded by the size of a largest non-redundant collection of subsets of $V$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the collection of all subsets of $V$. Based on $\mathcal{C}$, we construct such an undirected graph $\widehat{G}=(\mathcal{C},\widehat{E})$ where for any two nodes $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}, S_2 \in \mathcal{C} $, there is an edge connecting $S_1$ and $S_2$ iff $S_1 \subseteq S_2$ or $S_2 \subseteq S_1$. It can be verified that a sub-collection $\mathcal{C}^\prime \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ is a non-redundant iff $\mathcal{C}^\prime$ is an independent set in $\widehat{G}$. In Lemma~\ref{lem:maxiindep}, we show that $g(n)$ is the size of a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$, which implies that $g(n)$ is an upper bound for the number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: alpha-maximal cliques form a non-redundant collection = independent set in the inclusion graph on subsets; bound via Lemma 3.

nodes.name: Largest independent set C* of the inclusion graph
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}^*$ be a largest independent set in $\widehat{G}$.

nodes.name: Collection C_k of k-subsets
nodes.statement: Also, let $ \mathcal{C}_k\subseteq \mathcal{C} , 0 \le k \le n$ be the collection of subsets of $V$ with the size of $k$.

nodes.name: Each C_k is an independent set
nodes.statement: Observe that for each $0 \le k \le n$, $\mathcal{C}_k$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$.

nodes.name: L(n) and U(n)
nodes.statement: Also let $L(n)$ and $U(n)$ be respectively the minimum and maximum size of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$.

nodes.name: Size of a largest independent set of the inclusion graph
nodes.statement: For any $n \ge 3$, $\left | \mathcal{C}^* \right | = g(n)$.
nodes.label: lem:maxiindep

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3
nodes.statement: We first consider the case when $n$ is even. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:Lowe-n} and~\ref{lem:Upper-n}, we know $n/2 \le L(n) \le U(n) \le n/2$. Thus we have $L(n)=U(n)=n/2$ which implies $ \mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{n/2}$. Recall that $ \mathcal{C}_k\subseteq \mathcal{C} , 0 \le k \le n$ is the collection of subsets of $V$ with the size of $k$. We have (1)~$\mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{n/2} \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{n/2}$ and (2)~$|\mathcal{C}^*| \ge |\mathcal{C}_{n/2}| $ since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Thus we conclude $\mathcal{C}^*=\mathcal{C}_{n/2}$ which has the size of ${n \choose (n/2)} = g(n)$. We next consider the case when $n$ is odd. From Lemmas~\ref{lem:Lowe-n} and~\ref{lem:Upper-n}, we know $(n-1)/2 \le L(n) \le U(n) \le (n+1)/2$. Thus we have $ \mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{(n-1)/2} \bigcup \mathcal{C}^*_{(n+1)/2}$. For notation convenience, we set $n_1=(n-1)/2, n_2=(n+1)/2$. Let $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$ be the subgraph of $\widehat{G}$ induced by $\mathcal{C}_{n_1} \cup \mathcal{C}_{n_2}$. We can view $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$ as a bipartite graph with two disjoint vertex sets $\mathcal{C}_{n_1}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$ respectively. Observe that $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1} \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{n_1}$ and $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2} \subseteq\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$. Let $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ be the set of edges induced by $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}$ in $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$. Since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$, none of the edges in $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ will have an end in a node of $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}$, i.e, all the edges of $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ should have an end falling in $\mathcal{C}_{n_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}$. Note that in $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$, all nodes have a degree of $n_2$. Thus we have: $$ |\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})|=|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}|*n_2 \le |\mathcal{C}_{n_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}|*n_2= (|\mathcal{C}_{n_2}|-|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}|)*n_2 $$ from which we obtain $|\mathcal{C}^*|=|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}|+|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}| \le |\mathcal{C}_{n_2}|$ $=$ ${n} \choose n_2$. Note that $\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$ itself is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$ with size $n \choose n_2$. Thus we conclude that $|\mathcal{C}^*|$ $=$ ${n} \choose n_2$ $= g(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Case on parity of n: Lemmas 4-5 pin set sizes to the middle layer(s); for odd n a bipartite degree count bounds |C*|.

nodes.name: Lower bound on L(n)
nodes.statement: $L(n) \ge \lfloor n/2\rfloor$
assumptions: $L(n)$ and $U(n)$ be respectively the minimum and maximum size of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$
nodes.label: lem:Lowe-n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4
nodes.statement: Let us assume $n$ is an even number. We prove by contradiction as follows. Suppose $L(n)=\ell \le n/2-1$. Let $\mathcal{C}^*_k \subseteq \mathcal{C}^*, L(n)\le k \le U(n)$ be the collection of all sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$ which has the size of $k$, i.e, $\mathcal{C}^*_k =\{S \in \mathcal{C}^*| |S|=k\}$. In the following we construct a new collection $\mathcal{C}_{new} \subseteq \mathcal{C} $ which proves to be an independent set in $\widehat{G}$ with the size being strictly larger than $\mathcal{C}^*$. For each $S \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$, we add to $\mathcal{C}^*$ all subsets of $V$ which has the form as $S\cup \{i\}$ where $i \in V \setminus S$ and remove $S$ from $\mathcal{C}^*$ meanwhile. Let $\mathcal{C}_{new} $ be the collection obtained after we process the same route for all $S \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$. Mathematically, we have: $\mathcal{C}_{new}= \mathcal{C}_1 \bigcup \mathcal{C}_2$ where $\mathcal{C}_1=\bigcup_{S\in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell } \bigcup_{i \in V \setminus S} \{ S\cup \{i\} \}, \mathcal{C}_2=\mathcal{C}^* \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$. First we show $\mathcal{C}_{new} $ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Arbitrarily choose two distinct sets, say $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_{new}, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_{new}, S_1 \ne S_2$. We check all the possible cases one by one: \begin{itemize} \item $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_1$. We observe that $|S_1|=|S_2|=\ell+1$ and $S_1 \ne S_2$. Thus no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$. \item $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_2, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_2$. In this case no inclusion relation can exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$ since $\mathcal{C}_2$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. \item $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_2$. Since $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell$ is the collection of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$ which has the smallest size $\ell$, we get that $|S_2| \ge \ell+1=|S_1|$. Therefore there is only one possible inclusion relation existing here, that is $S_1 \subset S_2$. Suppose $S_1= S_1^\prime \cup \{i_1\} \subset S_2 $ for some $S_1^\prime \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$. Thus we get that $S_1^\prime \subset S_2$ which implies $\mathcal{C}^*$ is not an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Hence we conclude that no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$. \end{itemize} Summarizing the analysis above, we get that no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$ which yields $\mathcal{C}_{new} $ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Now we prove that $|\mathcal{C}_{new} |>|\mathcal{C}^* | $. Observe that $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ are disjoint from each other; otherwise $\mathcal{C}^*$ is not an independent set. So we have $|\mathcal{C}_{new}|=|\mathcal{C}_1|+|\mathcal{C}_2|$. Note that $|\mathcal{C}^*|=|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|+|\mathcal{C}_2|$ since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is the union of the two disjoint parts $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$. Therefore $|\mathcal{C}_{new} |>|\mathcal{C}^* | $ is equivalent to $|\mathcal{C}_1 |>|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell | $. Let $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ be the induced subgraph graph of $\widehat{G}$ by $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell \bigcup \mathcal{C}_1$. Note that $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ can be viewed as a bipartite graph where the two disjoint vertex sets are $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell $ and $\mathcal{C}_1$ respectively. In $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ we observe that (1) for each node $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$, its degree $d(S_1)=n-\ell$; (2) for each node $S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_1$, its degree $d(S_2) \le \ell+1$. Thus we get that $ |\widetilde{E}|=|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell| (n-\ell) \le |\mathcal{C}_1|(\ell+1) $. According to our assumption we have $\ell \le n/2-1$. Thus we have \\ $|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|/|\mathcal{C}_1| \le (\ell+1)/ (n-\ell) \le (n/2)/(n/2+1)<1$, yielding $|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|< |\mathcal{C}_1|$ which is equivalent to $|\mathcal{C}^* | < |\mathcal{C}_{new} | $. So far we have successfully constructed a new collection $\mathcal{C}_{new} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ such that (1) it is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$ and (2) $ |\mathcal{C}_{new} |>|\mathcal{C}^* |$. That contradicts with the fact that $\mathcal{C}^*$ is a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Thus our assumption $\ell \le n/2-1$ does not hold, which yields $\ell \ge n/2$. For the case when $n$ is odd, we can process essentially the same analysis as above and get $\ell \ge (n-1)/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: replacing the smallest sets by their one-element extensions yields a strictly larger independent set. The size gain follows from a bipartite degree count.

nodes.name: Upper bound on U(n)
nodes.statement: $U(n) \le \lceil n/2 \rceil $
assumptions: $L(n)$ and $U(n)$ be respectively the minimum and maximum size of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$
nodes.label: lem:Upper-n

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.statement: Let us assume $n$ is an even number. Based on $\mathcal{C}^*$, we construct a dual collection $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ as follows: Initialize $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ as an empty collection. For each $S\in \mathcal{C}^*$, we add $V \setminus S$ into $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$. Mathematically, we have: $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}=\bigcup_{S\in \mathcal{C}^*} \{V \setminus S\}$. First we show $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Arbitrarily choose two distinct sets, say $V \setminus S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*_{dual}, V \setminus S_2 \in \mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$, where $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}^*, S_1 \ne S_2$. Note that $$V \setminus S_1 \subset V \setminus S_2 \Leftrightarrow S_1 \supset S_2, V \setminus S_2 \subset V \setminus S_1 \Leftrightarrow S_2 \supset S_1 $$ Thus we have that no inclusion relation could exist between $V \setminus S_1$ and $V \setminus S_2$ since no inclusion relation exists between $S_1$ and $S_2$ resulting from the fact that $\mathcal{C}^*$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. So we get $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ is an independent set as well. We can verify that $|\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}|=|\mathcal{C}^*|$. Therefore we can conclude $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ is a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:Lowe-n}, we get to know the minimum size of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ should be at least $n/2$, which yields the maximum size of of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$ should be at most $n/2$. For the case when $n$ is odd, we can analyze essentially the same as above.
nodes.statement_short: Complementation maps C* to another largest independent set; apply Lemma 4 to it.

nodes.name: No edges with probability below alpha
nodes.statement: We assume that $\mathcal{G}$ has no edges $e$ such that $p(e) < \alpha$. If there are any such edges, they can be pruned away without losing any $\alpha$-maximal cliques, using Observation~\ref{obs:Elim}.

nodes.name: Vertex identifiers
nodes.statement: Let the vertex identifiers in $\mathcal{G}$ be $1,2,\ldots,n$.

nodes.name: max(C)
nodes.statement: For clique $C$, let $\max(C)$ denote the largest vertex in $C$.

nodes.name: Conventions for the empty set
nodes.statement: For ease of notation, let $\max(\emptyset) = 0$, and let $clq(\emptyset,\mathcal{G}) = 1$.

nodes.name: Basic DFS enumeration with backtracking
nodes.statement: We first describe a basic approach to enumeration using depth-first-search (DFS) with backtracking. The algorithm starts with a set of vertices $C$ (initialized to an empty set) that is an $\alpha$-clique and incrementally adds vertices to $C$, while retaining the property of $C$ being an $\alpha$-clique, until we can add no more vertices to $C$. At this point, we have an $\alpha$-maximal clique. Upon finding a clique that is $\alpha$-maximal, the algorithm backtracks to explore other possible vertices that can be used to extend $C$, until all possible search paths have been explored. To avoid exploring the same set $C$ more than once, we add vertices in increasing order of the vertex id. For instance, if $C$ was currently the vertex set $\{1,3,4\}$, we do not consider adding vertex $2$ to $C$, since the resulting clique $\{1,2,3,4\}$ will also be reached by the search path by adding vertices $1,2,3,4$ in that order.
nodes.statement_short: Depth-first search that grows an alpha-clique by adding vertices in increasing id order until it is maximal, then backtracks.

nodes.name: MULE
nodes.statement: \caption{MULE($\mathcal{G},\alpha$)} \KwIn{$\mathcal{G} \mbox{ is the input uncertain graph}$} \KwIn{$\alpha, 0 < \alpha < 1$ is the user provided probability threshold} $\hat{I} \leftarrow \emptyset$ \; \ForAll{$u \in V$} { $\hat{I} \leftarrow \hat{I} \cup \{ (u,1) \}$ } Enum-Uncertain-MC($\emptyset$, 1 ,$\hat{I}$, $\emptyset$) \;
input: $\alpha, 0 < \alpha < 1$ is the user provided probability threshold
nodes.statement_short: MULE: initialise candidate set with all vertices (factor 1) and call the recursive Enum-Uncertain-MC on the empty clique.
nodes.label: algo:main

nodes.name: Enum-Uncertain-MC
nodes.statement: \caption{Enum-Uncertain-MC($C,q,I,X$)} \KwIn{We assume $\mathcal{G}$ and $\alpha$ are available as immutable global variables} \KwIn{$C \mbox{ is the current Uncertain Clique being processed}$} \KwIn{$q = clq(C,\mathcal{G})$, maintained incrementally} \KwIn{$I \mbox{ is a set of all tuples} \left(u,r\right)$, such that $\forall (u,r) \in I$, $u > max(C)$, and $clq(C \cup \{ u\},\mathcal{G}) = q \cdot r \ge \alpha$, i.e. $C \cup \{ u \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$} \KwIn{$X \mbox{ is a set of all tuples} \left(v,s\right)$, such that $\forall (v,s) \in X$, $v \not \in C$, $v < max(C)$, and $clq(C \cup \{v\},\mathcal{G}) = q \cdot s \ge \alpha$ , i.e. $C \cup \{ v \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$} \If{$I = \emptyset$ and $X = \emptyset$} { Output $C$ as $\alpha$-maximal clique \; \Return } \ForAll{$ (u,r) \in I$ considered in increasing order of $u$} { $C' \leftarrow C \cup \{ u \}$ \tcp{Note $m = max(C') = u$} $q' \leftarrow q \cdot r$ \tcp{$clq(C \cup \{ v \},\mathcal{G})$} $I' \leftarrow GenerateI(C',q',I)$ \; $X' \leftarrow GenerateX(C',q',X)$ \; Enum-Uncertain-MC($C',q',I',X')$ \; $X \leftarrow X \cup \{ (u,r) \}$ }
input: $C \mbox{ is the current Uncertain Clique being processed}$
nodes.statement_short: Recursive DFS: output C when no extending vertex remains in I or X; else extend by each u in I, updating I and X incrementally.
nodes.label: algo:dfs

nodes.name: GenerateI
nodes.statement: \caption{GenerateI($C',q',I$)} \KwIn{We assume $\mathcal{G}$ and $\alpha$ are available as immutable global variables} $m \leftarrow max(C')$, $I' \leftarrow \emptyset$, $S \leftarrow \emptyset$ \; \ForAll{$(u,r) \in I$} { $S \leftarrow S \cup \{ u \}$ } $S \leftarrow S \cap \{ \Gamma(m) \}$ \ForAll{$(u,r) \in I$} { \If{$u > m$ and $u \in S$} { $clq(C' \cup\{ u \},\mathcal{G}) \leftarrow q' \cdot r \cdot p(\{u,m\})$ \If{$(clq(C' \cup\{ u \},\mathcal{G})) \ge \alpha$} { $u' \leftarrow u$ \; $r' \leftarrow r \cdot p(\{u,m\})$ \; $I' \leftarrow I' \cup \{ (u',r') \}$ } } } \Return I'
nodes.statement_short: Build the new candidate set I' from I: keep neighbours of m larger than m whose updated clique probability stays >= alpha.
nodes.label: algo:generateI

nodes.name: GenerateX
nodes.statement: \caption{GenerateX($C',q',X$)} \KwIn{We assume $\mathcal{G}$ and $\alpha$ are available as immutable global variables} $m \leftarrow max(C')$, $X' \leftarrow \emptyset$, $S \leftarrow \emptyset$ \; \ForAll{$(v,s) \in I$} { $S \leftarrow S \cup \{ v \}$ } $S \leftarrow S \cap \{ \Gamma(m) \}$ \ForAll{$(v,s) \in X$} { \If{$v \in S$} { $clq(C' \cup\{ v \},\mathcal{G}) \leftarrow q' \cdot s \cdot p(\{v,m\})$ \If{$(clq(C' \cup\{ v \},\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$} { $v' \leftarrow v$ \; $s' \leftarrow s \cdot p(\{v,m\})$ \; $X' \leftarrow X' \cup \{ (v',s') \}$ } } } \Return X'
nodes.statement_short: Build the new exclusion set X' from X: keep neighbours of m whose updated clique probability stays >= alpha.
nodes.label: algo:generateX

nodes.name: Correctness of MULE
nodes.statement: MULE (Algorithm~\ref{algo:main}) enumerates all $\alpha$-maximal cliques from an input uncertain graph $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.label: thm:correctness

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: To prove the theorem we need to show the following. First, if $C$ is a clique emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:main}, then $C$ must be an $\alpha$-maximal clique. Next, if $C$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique, then it will be emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:main}. We prove them in Lemmas~\ref{lemma:correctness1}~and~\ref{lemma:correctness2} respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Soundness and completeness are Lemmas 8 and 9.

nodes.name: Invariant of the candidate set I'
nodes.statement: When Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} is called with $C'$ in line~\ref{algoline:recursion}, $I'$ is a set of all tuples $(u'r')$, where $u' \in V$ and $0 < r' \le 1$, such that, $\forall (u',r') \in I'$ , $u' > max(C')$, and $clq(C' \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot r' \ge \alpha$, i.e. $C' \cup \{ u' \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$.
assumptions: Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} is called with $C'$ in line~\ref{algoline:recursion}
conclusions: $I'$ is a set of all tuples $(u'r')$, where $u' \in V$ and $0 < r' \le 1$, such that, $\forall (u',r') \in I'$ , $u' > max(C')$, and $clq(C' \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot r' \ge \alpha$, i.e. $C' \cup \{ u' \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement_short: I' holds exactly the larger vertices u' extending C' to an alpha-clique, with factors r' such that clq = q' r'.
nodes.label: obs:I

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6
nodes.statement: Let $u' \in V$ be a vertex such that (1)~$u' > \max(C')$, and (2)~$C' \cup \{ u' \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. We need to show that $(u',r') \in I'$ such that $clq(C' \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot r'$. Let $C'$ be a clique being called by Enum-Uncertain-MC with $I'$. Note that each call of the method adds one vertex $u \in I$ to the current clique $C$ such $u > \max(C)$. Since the vertices are added in the lexicographical ordering, there is an unique sequence of calls to the method Enum-Uncertain-MC such that we reach a point in execution of Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} where Enum-Uncertain-MC is called with $C'$. We call this sequence of calls as Call-$0$, Call-$1$, $\ldots$, Call-$\left | C' \right |$. Also, let $C_i$ be the clique used by method Enum-Uncertain-MC during Call-$i$. We prove by induction. First consider the base case. For that consider the first call made to Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}, i.e. Call-$0$. We know that $C$ is initialized as $\emptyset$. During the first call made, all vertices in $V$ satisfy conditions (1) and (2). This is because, first $max(\emptyset) = 0$. Second any single vertex can be considered as a clique with probability $1$. $\hat{I}$ is initialized such that all $r$ in $\hat{I}$ are $1 \ge \alpha$. Thus for all u such that $(u,r) \in \hat{I}$, $u > \max(C)$. This proves the base case. For the inductive step, consider a recursive call to the method Call-$i$ which calls Call-$(i+1)$. For every case expect initialization, $I'$ is generated from $I$ by line~\ref{algoline:genI} of Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} which in turn calls Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}. In Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}, only vertices in $I$ that are greater than $C'$ are added to $I'$. Thus all vertices in $I$ that satisfy (1) are added to $I'$. Next every vertex in $I$ is connected to $C$. We need to show that all vertices in $I'$ are connected to $C'$. In line 4 of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}, we prune out any vertex in $I$ that is not connected to $m = \max(C')$. Assume that $u'$ extends $C$ such that $clq(C \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = r$. Now let $c = \{ C' \setminus C$ \}. Note that $c$ is a single vertex. Also, assume $u' > c$. From line 4, we know that $q' \cdot r' \ge \alpha$ Also from line 6 of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}, $r' = r \cdot p(\{c,u'\})$. Now $clq(C' \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot r \cdot p(\{c,u'\}) = q' \cdot r'$, Now in line 8 of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI} we add $u'$ to $I'$ only if $r' \ge \alpha$ thus proving the inductive step.
nodes.statement_short: Induction along the unique call sequence reaching C'; GenerateI keeps exactly the valid extensions with updated factors.

nodes.name: Proof of Observation 4
nodes.statement: The following observation follows from Lemma~\ref{obs:I}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Lemma 6.

nodes.name: Input of Enum-Uncertain-MC is an alpha-clique
nodes.statement: The input $C$ to Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} is an $\alpha$-clique.
conclusions: The input $C$ to Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} is an $\alpha$-clique
nodes.label: obs:cliqueprob

nodes.name: Invariant of the exclusion set X'
nodes.statement: When Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} is called with $C'$ in line~\ref{algoline:recursion}, $X'$ is a set of all tuples $(v',s')$, where $v' \in V$ and $0 < s' \le 1$, such that, $\forall (v',s') \in X'$, we have $v' \not \in C'$, $v' < \max(C')$, and $(clq(C' \cup \{ v' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot s') \ge \alpha$, i.e. $C' \cup \{ v' \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$.
assumptions: Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} is called with $C'$ in line~\ref{algoline:recursion}
conclusions: $X'$ is a set of all tuples $(v',s')$, where $v' \in V$ and $0 < s' \le 1$, such that, $\forall (v',s') \in X'$, we have $v' \not \in C'$, $v' < \max(C')$, and $(clq(C' \cup \{ v' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot s') \ge \alpha$, i.e. $C' \cup \{ v' \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement_short: X' holds exactly the smaller non-member vertices extending C' to an alpha-clique, with factors s' such that clq = q' s'.
nodes.label: obs:X

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.statement:
Let $m = \max(C')$ and $C = C' \setminus \{ m\}$. Since Algorithm~ef{algo:dfs} was called with $C'$, it must have been called with $C$. This is because the working clique is always extended by adding vertices from $I$, and from Lemma~ef{obs:I}, $I$ only contains vertices that are greater than the maximum vertex in $C$. Let $X$ be the corresponding set of tuples used when the call was made to Enum-Uncertain-MC with $C$. Let $u > \max(C)$ be a vertex such that $clq(C' \cup \{ u \},\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$ and $u < m$. Note that $u 
ot \in C'$, $u < \max(C')$, and $C' \cup \{ u \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. This means $u$ satisfies all conditions for $u \in X'$. We need to show that when Enum-Uncertain-MC is called with $C'$, the generated $X'$ which is passed in Enum-Uncertain-MC contains $u$. Firstly, note that since $C' \cup \{ u \}$ is $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$, we have $clq(C \cup \{ u \},\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$ (from Observation~ef{obs:Sub}). Since $u > \max(C)$ and $clq(C \cup \{ u \},\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$, from Lemma~ef{obs:I}, $u$ will be used in line~ef{algoline:loop} to call Enum-Uncertain-MC using $C \cup \{ u \}$. Once this call is returned, $u$ is added to $X$ in line~ef{algoline:addX}. Note that since the loop at line~ef{algoline:loop} add vertices in lexicographical order, $m$ will be added to $C$ after $u$. Thus $u$ will be in $X$, when $m$ is used to extend $C$. Next we show that if $u \in X$, after execution of line~ef{algoline:genX}, $u \in X'$. We prove this as follows. Note that Algorithm~ef{algo:generateX} is used to generate $X'$ from $X$. Note that $X'$ is generated by Algorithm~ef{algo:generateX} by selectively adding vertices from $X$. A vertex is added to $X'$ from $X$, only if $C' \cup \{ u \}$ is $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. From our initial assumptions, we know that $u$ satisfies this condition and is hence added to $X'$ and passed on to Enum-Uncertain-MC when it is called with $C'$. Now let us consider $v$, such that $v$ does not satisfy all the conditions for $v \in X'$. We need to show that $v 
ot \in X'$. There are two cases. First, when $v 
ot \in X$. This case is trivial as $X'$ is constructed from $X$ and hence if $v 
ot \in X$, $v 
ot \in X'$. For the second case, when $v \in X$, we need to show that $v$ will not be added to $X'$ in line~ef{algoline:genX} of Algorithm~ef{algo:dfs}. Note that since $v \in X$, we know $v 
ot \in C'$ and $v < \max(C')$. Thus, it must be that $C \cup \{ m, v \}$ is not an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. Algorithm~ef{algo:generateX} will add $v$ to $X'$ only if $C \cup \{ m, v \}$ is $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. But from our previous discussion, we know that this condition doesn't hold. Hence, $v$ will not be added to $X'$. Thus only vertices that satisfy all three conditions are in $X'$.
nodes.statement_short: Track a valid smaller vertex u into X then X' via the loop order and GenerateX; show invalid v are never added, by two cases.

nodes.name: Soundness of Enum-Uncertain-MC
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a clique emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}. Then $C$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique.
assumptions: $C$ be a clique emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}
nodes.label: lemma:correctness1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} emits $C$ in Line~\ref{algoline:out}. From Observation~\ref{obs:cliqueprob}, we know that $C$ is an $\alpha$-clique. We need to show that $C$ is $\alpha$-maximal. We use proof by contradiction. Suppose $C$ is non-maximal. This means that there exists a vertex $u \in V$, such that $C \cup \{u\}$ is an $\alpha$-clique. We know that $I = \emptyset$ when $C$ is emitted. From Lemma~\ref{obs:I}, we know that there exists no vertex $u \in V$ such that $u > max(C)$ that can extend $C$. Again, we know that $X = \emptyset$ when $C$ is emitted. Thus from Lemma~\ref{obs:X}, we know that there exists no vertex $v \in V$ such that $v < \max(C)$ that can extend $C$. This is a contradiction and hence $C$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: an extending vertex would lie in I or X by Lemmas 6-7, but both are empty when C is emitted.

nodes.name: Completeness of Enum-Uncertain-MC
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be an $\alpha$-maximal clique in $\mathcal{G}$. Then $C$ is emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}.
nodes.label: lemma:correctness2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.statement: We first show that a call to method Enum-Uncertain-MC with $\alpha$-clique $C$ enumerates all $\alpha$-maximal cliques $C'$ in $\mathcal{G}$, such that for all $c \in \{ C' \setminus C \}$, $c > \max(C)$. Without loss of generality, consider a $\alpha$-maximal clique $C'$ in $\mathcal{G}$ such that $\forall c \in \{C' \setminus C \}$, $c > \max(C)$. Note that $C'$ will be emitted as an $\alpha$-maximal clique by the method Enum-Uncertain-MC when called with $C$, if the following holds: (1) A call to method Enum-Uncertain-MC is made with $C'$, (2) When this call is made, $I' = \emptyset$, and $X' = \emptyset$. Since $C'$ is $\alpha$-maximal clique in $\mathcal{G}$, the second point follows from Lemmas~\ref{obs:I}~and~\ref{obs:X}. Thus we need to show that a call to Enum-Uncertain-MC is made with $C'$. We prove this by induction. Let $\hat{C} = \{ C' \setminus C \}$. Let $c_i$ represent the $i$th element in $\hat{C}$ in lexicographical order. Also let $C_i = C \cup \{ c_{1}, c_{2}, \ldots, c_i \}$. For the base case, we show that if a call to Enum-Uncertain-MC is made with $C$, a call will be made with $C_1 = C \cup \{ c_1 \}$. This is because, line~\ref{algoline:loop} of the method loops over every vertex $u \in I$ thus implying $u > \max(C)$ and $clq(C \cup \{ u \},\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$. Since $C'$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique, $c_1$ will satisfy both these conditions and hence a call to Enum-Uncertain-MC is made with $C \cup \{ c_1 \}$. Now for the inductive step we show that if a call is made with clique $C_i$, then this call will in turn call the method with clique $C_{i+1}$. Again, $c_{i+1}$ is greater than $\max(C_i)$ and $clq(C_i \cup \{ c_{i+1} \},\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$. Thus $c_{i+1} \in I$ when the call is made to Enum-Uncertain-MC with $C_i$. Hence using the previous argument, in line~\ref{algoline:loop}, $c_{i+1}$ will be used as a vertex in the loop which would in turn make a call to Enum-Uncertain-MC with $C_{i+1}$. Now without any loss of generality, consider an $\alpha$-maximal clique in $\mathcal{G}$. We know that $C \supset \emptyset$. Thus the proof follows.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the vertices of C' \ C in increasing order shows the search reaches C'; Lemmas 6-7 give empty I', X' there.

nodes.name: Runtime of MULE
nodes.statement: The runtime of MULE (Algorithm~\ref{algo:main}) on an input graph of $n$ vertices is $O\left (n \cdot 2^n \right)$.
conclusions: The runtime of MULE (Algorithm~\ref{algo:main}) on an input graph of $n$ vertices is $O\left (n \cdot 2^n \right)$
also_stated_at: We present a theoretical analysis showing that the worst-case runtime of MULE is $O(n \cdot 2^{n})$, where $n$ is the number of vertices.
nodes.label: thm:complexity

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: MULE initializes variables and calls to Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}, hence we analyze the runtime of Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}. An execution of the recursive Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} can be viewed as a search tree as follows. Each call to Enum-Uncertain-MC is a node of this search tree. The first call to the method is the root node. A node in this search tree is either an internal node that makes one or more recursive calls, or a leaf node that does not make further recursive calls. To analyze the runtime of Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}, we consider the time spent at internal nodes as well as leaf nodes. The runtime at each leaf node is $O(1)$. For a leaf node, the parameter $I = \emptyset$, and there are no further recursive calls. This implies that either $C$ is $\alpha$-maximal ($X = \emptyset$) and is emitted in line~\ref{algoline:out} or it is non-maximal ($X \neq \emptyset$) but cannot be extended by the loop in line~\ref{algoline:loop} as $I = \emptyset$. Checking the sizes of $I$ and $X$ takes constant time. We next consider the time taken at each internal node. Instead of adding up the times at different internal nodes, we equivalently add up the cost of the different edges in the search tree. At each internal node, the cost of making a recursive call can be analyzed as follows. Line~\ref{algoline:genc} takes $O \left ( n \right )$ time as we add all vertices in $C$ to $C'$ and also $u$. Line~\ref{algoline:prob} takes constant time. Lines~\ref{algoline:genI}~and~\ref{algoline:genX} take $O \left ( n \right )$ time (Lemmas~\ref{lemma:complexity1}~and~\ref{lemma:complexity2} respectively). Note that lines~\ref{algoline:genc}~to~\ref{algoline:genX} can get executed only once in between the two calls. Thus total runtime for each edge of the search tree is $O\left ( n \right )$. Note that the total number of calls made to the method method Enum-Uncertain-MC is no more than the possible number of unique subsets of $V$, which is $O \left ( 2^n \right )$. We see that for internal nodes, time complexity is $O \left ( n \right )$ and for leaf nodes it is $O \left ( 1 \right )$. Hence the time complexity of Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} is $O \left ( n \cdot 2^n \right )$.
nodes.statement_short: Search-tree accounting: O(1) per leaf, O(n) per tree edge (Lemmas 10-11), at most 2^n calls.

nodes.name: Runtime of GenerateI
nodes.statement: The runtime of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI} is $O \left ( n \right )$.
conclusions: The runtime of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI} is $O \left ( n \right )$
nodes.label: lemma:complexity1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: First note that lines 1-6 takes $O \left ( n \right )$ time. This is because $\left | I \right | = O \left ( n \right )$, and hence the loop at line 4 of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI} can take $O \left ( n \right )$ time. Further the set intersection at line 6 also takes $O \left ( n \right )$ time. We need to show that the for loop in line 7 is $O \left ( n \right )$, that is each iteration of the loop takes $O \left ( 1 \right )$ time. Assume that it takes constant time to find out the probability of an edge. This is a valid assumption, as the edge probabilities can be stored as a HashMap and hence for an edge $e$, in constant time we can find out $p(e)$. With this assumption, it is easy to show that lines 8-13 takes constant time. This is because, they are either constant number of multiplications, or adding one element to a set. Thus total time complexity is $O \left ( n \right )$.
nodes.statement_short: Line-by-line cost count, assuming O(1) edge-probability lookup via a hash map.

nodes.name: Runtime of GenerateX
nodes.statement: The runtime of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateX} is $O \left ( n \right )$.
conclusions: The runtime of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateX} is $O \left ( n \right )$
nodes.label: lemma:complexity2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 11 (omitted)
nodes.statement: We omit the proof of the above lemma since it is similar to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:complexity1}.
nodes.statement_short: Omitted; analogous to the proof of Lemma 10.

nodes.name: Lower bound on enumeration runtime
nodes.statement: The worst-case runtime of any algorithm that can output all maximal cliques of an uncertain graph on $n$ vertices is $\Omega \left ( \sqrt{n} \cdot 2^n \right )$.
conclusions: The worst-case runtime of any algorithm that can output all maximal cliques of an uncertain graph on $n$ vertices is $\Omega \left ( \sqrt{n} \cdot 2^n \right )$
nodes.label: obs:opt

nodes.name: Proof of Observation 5
nodes.statement: From Theorem~\ref{thm:maximum}, we know that the number of maximal uncertain cliques can be as much as ${n \choose \lfloor n/2 \rfloor} = \Theta \left (\frac{{2^n}}{\sqrt{n}} \right )$ (using Stirling's Approximation). Since the size of each uncertain clique can be $\Theta\left ( n \right )$, the total output size can be $\Omega \left ( \sqrt{n} \cdot 2^n \right )$, which is a lower bound on the runtime of any algorithm.
nodes.statement_short: Output-size bound: Theorem 1 with Stirling gives Theta(2^n/sqrt n) cliques of size Theta(n).

nodes.name: Near-optimality of MULE
nodes.statement: The worst-case runtime of MULE on an $n$ vertex graph is within a $O(\sqrt{n})$ factor of the runtime of an optimal algorithm for Maximal Clique Enumeration on an uncertain graph.
conclusions: The worst-case runtime of MULE on an $n$ vertex graph is within a $O(\sqrt{n})$ factor of the runtime of an optimal algorithm for Maximal Clique Enumeration on an uncertain graph
nodes.label: obs:timefactor

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 12
nodes.statement: The proof follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:complexity} and Observation~\ref{obs:opt}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare Theorem 3's upper bound with Observation 5's lower bound.

nodes.name: Shared Neighborhood Filtering
nodes.statement: As a first step, we prune the input uncertain graph $\mathcal{G} = (V,E,p)$ by employing techniques described by Modani and Dey~\cite{Modani08}. We apply the ``Shared Neighborhood Filtering" where edges are recursively checked and removed as follows. First drop all edges $\{u,v\} \in E$, such that $\left | \Gamma(u) \cap \Gamma(v) \right | < (t-2)$. Next drop every vertex $v \in V$, that doesn't satisfy the following condition. For vertex $v \in V$, there must exist at least $(t-1)$ vertices in $\Gamma(v)$, such that for $u \in \Gamma(v)$, $\left | \Gamma(u) \cap \Gamma(v) \right | < (t-2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Pruning: drop edges whose endpoints share fewer than t-2 neighbours, then drop vertices without enough such neighbours.

nodes.name: Pruned graph G'
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{G}'$ denote the graph resulting from $\mathcal{G}$ after the pruning step.

nodes.name: LARGE-MULE
nodes.statement: \caption{LARGE--MULE($\mathcal{G},\alpha$,$t$)} \KwIn{$\mathcal{G}' \mbox{ is the input uncertain graph post pruning}$} \KwIn{$\alpha, 0 < \alpha < 1$ is the user provided probability threshold} \KwIn{$t, t \ge 2$ is the user provided size threshold} $\hat{I} \leftarrow \emptyset$ \; \ForAll{$u \in V$} { $\hat{I} \leftarrow \hat{I} \cup \{ (u,1) \}$ } Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large($\emptyset$, 1 ,$\hat{I}$, $\emptyset$,$t$) \;
input: $\mathcal{G}' \mbox{ is the input uncertain graph post pruning}$
$t, t \ge 2$ is the user provided size threshold
nodes.statement_short: LARGE-MULE: initialise the candidate set and call Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large on the pruned graph with size threshold t.
nodes.label: algo:largemule

nodes.name: Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large
nodes.statement: \caption{Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large($C,q,I,X$,$t$)} \KwIn{$C \mbox{ is the current Uncertain Clique being processed}$} \KwIn{$q \mbox{ is pre-computed } clq(C,\mathcal{G})$} \KwIn{$I \mbox{ is a set of tuples} \left(u,r\right)$, such that $\forall (u,r) \in I$, $u > \max(C)$, and $clq(C \cup \{ u\},\mathcal{G}) = q \cdot r \ge \alpha$, i.e. $C \cup \{ u \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$} \KwIn{$X \mbox{ is a set of tuples} \left(v,s\right)$, such that $\forall (v,s) \in X$, $v \not \in C$, $v < \max(C)$, and $clq(C \cup \{v\},\mathcal{G}) = q \cdot s \ge \alpha$ , i.e. $C \cup \{ v \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$} \KwIn{$t \mbox{ is the user provided size threshold}$} \If{$I = \emptyset$ and $X = \emptyset$} { Output $C$ as $\alpha$-maximal clique \; \Return } \ForAll{$u,r \in I$ taken in lexicographical ordering of $u$} { $C' \leftarrow C \cup \{ u \}$ \tcp{Note $m = \max(C') = u$} $q' \leftarrow q \cdot r$ \tcp{$clq(C \cup \{ v \},\mathcal{G})$} $I' \leftarrow GenerateI(C',q',I)$ \; \If{$\left | C' \right | + \left | I' \right | < t$} { continue \; } $X' \leftarrow GenerateX(C',q',X)$ \; Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large($C',q',I',X',t)$ \; $X \leftarrow X \cup \{ (u,r) \}$ }
input: $t \mbox{ is the user provided size threshold}$
nodes.statement_short: Enum-Uncertain-MC with an extra cut: skip a branch when |C'|+|I'| < t.
nodes.label: algo:large

nodes.name: Correctness of LARGE-MULE
nodes.statement: Given an input graph $\mathcal{G}$, LARGE--MULE (Algorithm~\ref{algo:largemule}) enumerates every $\alpha$-maximal clique with more than $t$ vertices.
conclusions: LARGE--MULE (Algorithm~\ref{algo:largemule}) enumerates every $\alpha$-maximal clique with more than $t$ vertices
nodes.label: lem:large

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: First we prove that no maximal clique of size less than $t$ is enumerated by Algorithm~\ref{algo:large}. Consider an $\alpha$-maximal clique $C_1$ in $\mathcal{G}$ with less than $t$ vertices. Also let $m_1 = \max(C_1)$ and $C_1' = C_1 \setminus \{ m_1 \}$. Note that if $C_1$ is emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:large}, then a call must be made to Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large with $C_1$. Since the Algorithm adds vertices in lexicographical ordering, this implies that a call must be made to Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large with $C_1'$ before the call is made with $C_1$. In the worst case, let us consider that the search tree reaches the execution point where Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large is called with $C_1'$. Consider the execution of the algorithm where $m_1$ is added to $C = C_1'$ to form $C' = C_1$. Since $C_1$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique, $I'$ will become NULL which implies $\left | I' \right | = 0$. We know that $\left | C_1 \right | < t$. Thus $\left | C_1 + I' \right |$ will also be less than $t$ and the If condition (line 8) will succeed. This will result in the execution of the continue statement. Thus Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large will not be called with $C_1$ implying that $C_1$ is not enumerated. Next we show that any maximal clique of size at least $t$ is enumerated by Algorithm~\ref{algo:large}. Consider an $\alpha$-maximal clique $C_2$ in $\mathcal{G}$ of size at least $t$. We note that the ``If'' condition in line 8 is never satisfied in the search path ending with $C_2$ and hence a call is made to the method with Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large with $C_2$. This is easy to see as whenever a call is made to Enum-Uncertain-MC-Large with any $C \subseteq C_2$, since $C_2$ is large, we always have $\left | C \right | + \left | I \right | \ge t$.
nodes.statement_short: Small maximal cliques are cut by the |C'|+|I'|<t test; large ones never trigger it along their search path.

nodes.name: DFS-NOIP
nodes.statement: \caption{DFS--NOIP($C$,$I$)} $I_{copy} \leftarrow I$ \; \ForAll{$u \in I_{copy}$} { \If{$u \le max(C)$ OR $clq(C \cup \{ u \}) < \alpha$} { $I \leftarrow I \setminus \{ u \}$ } } \If{$I = \emptyset$} { \If{$C$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique} { Output $C$ as $\alpha$-maximal clique \; \Return \; } } \ForAll{$v \in I$} { $C' \leftarrow C \cup \{ v \}$ \; \If{$C'$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique} { Output $C'$ as $\alpha$-maximal clique \; } \Else { $I' \leftarrow I \cap \Gamma( v )$ \; DFS--NOIP($C'$,$I'$) \; } }
nodes.statement_short: Baseline DFS for alpha-maximal cliques that recomputes clique probabilities instead of maintaining them incrementally.
nodes.label: algo:naive

nodes.name: MULE outperforms DFS-NOIP
nodes.statement: The results show that MULE performs much better than DFS--NOIP.

nodes.name: Number of alpha-maximal cliques is not monotone in alpha
nodes.statement: We note that the number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques does not have to always decrease as $\alpha$ increases. Sometimes it is possible that the number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques increases with $\alpha$. This is because as $\alpha$ increases, a large maximal clique may split into many smaller maximal cliques.

nodes.name: Runtime proportional to output size
nodes.statement: It can be seen that the runtime of the algorithm is almost proportional to the number of maximal cliques in the output.

nodes.name: Worst-case optimal uncertain maximal clique enumeration
nodes.statement: An interesting open problem is to design an algorithm for enumerating maximal cliques from an uncertain graph whose time complexity is worst-case optimal, $O \left ( \sqrt{n} \cdot 2^n \right)$.

nodes.name: Sample a graph
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a graph sampled from $\mathcal{G}$. The set $C$ will be a clique in $G$ iff every edge in $E_C$ is present in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: C is a clique in a sample iff all edges of E_C are present.

nodes.name: Independence gives product
nodes.statement: Since the events of selecting different edges are independent of each other, the observation follows.
nodes.statement_short: Independence of edges gives the product formula.

nodes.name: Construct the uncertain graph
nodes.statement: First, we assume that $n$ is even. Consider $\mathcal{G} = (V,E,p)$, where $E = V \times V$. Let $\mbox{$\kappa = {{n/2} \choose 2}$}$. For each $e \in E$, let $p(e)=q$ where $q^{\kappa}=\alpha$. We have $0 <q <1$ since $0< \alpha <1$.
nodes.statement_short: For even n, take the complete graph with all edge probabilities q, q^kappa = alpha.

nodes.name: Half-size sets are alpha-maximal
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an arbitrary subset of $V$ such that $|S|=n/2$. We can verify that $S$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique since (1)~the probability that $S$ is a clique is $q^{\kappa}=\alpha$ and (2)~for any set $S^\prime \supsetneq S, S^\prime \subseteq V$, the probability that $S^\prime$ is a clique is at most $q q^{\kappa}=q\alpha <\alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Every n/2-subset is an alpha-clique and no superset is.

nodes.name: Other sizes fail
nodes.statement: We can also observe that for any subset $S \subseteq V$, $S$ cannot be an $\alpha$-maximal clique if $|S|< n/2$ or $|S|> n/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Sets of other sizes are not alpha-maximal.

nodes.name: Count
nodes.statement: Thus we conclude that a subset $S\subseteq V$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique iff $|S|=n/2$ which implies that the total number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$ is $n \choose {n/2}$. A similar proof applies when $n$ is odd.
nodes.statement_short: Exactly the n/2-subsets are alpha-maximal: C(n,n/2) of them; odd n similar.

nodes.name: Collection of alpha-maximal cliques
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}^{\alpha}(\mathcal{G})$ be the collection of all $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$. Note that by the definition of $\alpha$-maximal cliques, any $\alpha$-maximal clique $S$ in $\mathcal{G}$ can not be a proper subset of any other $\alpha$-maximal clique in $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: No alpha-maximal clique is a proper subset of another.

nodes.name: Reduce to non-redundant collections
nodes.statement: Thus from Definition~\ref{defn:non-redundant}, for any uncertain graph $\mathcal{G}$, $\mathcal{C}^{\alpha}(\mathcal{G})$ is a non-redundant collection. Hence, it is clear that the largest number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$ should be upper bounded by the size of a largest non-redundant collection of subsets of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to bounding the largest non-redundant collection.

nodes.name: Inclusion graph
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be the collection of all subsets of $V$. Based on $\mathcal{C}$, we construct such an undirected graph $\widehat{G}=(\mathcal{C},\widehat{E})$ where for any two nodes $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}, S_2 \in \mathcal{C} $, there is an edge connecting $S_1$ and $S_2$ iff $S_1 \subseteq S_2$ or $S_2 \subseteq S_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the inclusion graph on all subsets of V.

nodes.name: Non-redundant = independent
nodes.statement: It can be verified that a sub-collection $\mathcal{C}^\prime \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ is a non-redundant iff $\mathcal{C}^\prime$ is an independent set in $\widehat{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-redundant collections are independent sets of the inclusion graph.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3
nodes.statement: In Lemma~\ref{lem:maxiindep}, we show that $g(n)$ is the size of a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$, which implies that $g(n)$ is an upper bound for the number of $\alpha$-maximal cliques in $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3 bounds the largest independent set by g(n).

nodes.name: Case n even
nodes.statement: We first consider the case when $n$ is even. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:Lowe-n} and~\ref{lem:Upper-n}, we know $n/2 \le L(n) \le U(n) \le n/2$. Thus we have $L(n)=U(n)=n/2$ which implies $ \mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{n/2}$. Recall that $ \mathcal{C}_k\subseteq \mathcal{C} , 0 \le k \le n$ is the collection of subsets of $V$ with the size of $k$. We have (1)~$\mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{n/2} \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{n/2}$ and (2)~$|\mathcal{C}^*| \ge |\mathcal{C}_{n/2}| $ since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Thus we conclude $\mathcal{C}^*=\mathcal{C}_{n/2}$ which has the size of ${n \choose (n/2)} = g(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Even n: C* is the middle layer.

nodes.name: Apply Lemmas 4 and 5
nodes.statement: We first consider the case when $n$ is even. By Lemmas~\ref{lem:Lowe-n} and~\ref{lem:Upper-n}, we know $n/2 \le L(n) \le U(n) \le n/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 4-5 give n/2 <= L(n) <= U(n) <= n/2.

nodes.name: All sets have size n/2
nodes.statement: Thus we have $L(n)=U(n)=n/2$ which implies $ \mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{n/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: So C* consists of n/2-sets.

nodes.name: Recall C_k
nodes.statement: Recall that $ \mathcal{C}_k\subseteq \mathcal{C} , 0 \le k \le n$ is the collection of subsets of $V$ with the size of $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of C_k.

nodes.name: Compare with C_{n/2}
nodes.statement: We have (1)~$\mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{n/2} \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{n/2}$ and (2)~$|\mathcal{C}^*| \ge |\mathcal{C}_{n/2}| $ since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: C* is contained in C_{n/2} and is at least as large.

nodes.name: C* = C_{n/2}
nodes.statement: Thus we conclude $\mathcal{C}^*=\mathcal{C}_{n/2}$ which has the size of ${n \choose (n/2)} = g(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence |C*| = C(n,n/2) = g(n).

nodes.name: Case n odd
nodes.statement: We next consider the case when $n$ is odd. From Lemmas~\ref{lem:Lowe-n} and~\ref{lem:Upper-n}, we know $(n-1)/2 \le L(n) \le U(n) \le (n+1)/2$. Thus we have $ \mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{(n-1)/2} \bigcup \mathcal{C}^*_{(n+1)/2}$. For notation convenience, we set $n_1=(n-1)/2, n_2=(n+1)/2$. Let $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$ be the subgraph of $\widehat{G}$ induced by $\mathcal{C}_{n_1} \cup \mathcal{C}_{n_2}$. We can view $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$ as a bipartite graph with two disjoint vertex sets $\mathcal{C}_{n_1}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$ respectively. Observe that $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1} \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{n_1}$ and $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2} \subseteq\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$. Let $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ be the set of edges induced by $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}$ in $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$. Since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$, none of the edges in $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ will have an end in a node of $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}$, i.e, all the edges of $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ should have an end falling in $\mathcal{C}_{n_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}$. Note that in $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$, all nodes have a degree of $n_2$. Thus we have: $$ |\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})|=|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}|*n_2 \le |\mathcal{C}_{n_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}|*n_2= (|\mathcal{C}_{n_2}|-|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}|)*n_2 $$ from which we obtain $|\mathcal{C}^*|=|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}|+|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}| \le |\mathcal{C}_{n_2}|$ $=$ ${n} \choose n_2$. Note that $\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$ itself is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$ with size $n \choose n_2$. Thus we conclude that $|\mathcal{C}^*|$ $=$ ${n} \choose n_2$ $= g(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Odd n: bipartite degree count between the two middle layers.

nodes.name: Apply Lemmas 4 and 5
nodes.statement: We next consider the case when $n$ is odd. From Lemmas~\ref{lem:Lowe-n} and~\ref{lem:Upper-n}, we know $(n-1)/2 \le L(n) \le U(n) \le (n+1)/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Set sizes lie in the two middle layers.

nodes.name: C* in two layers
nodes.statement: Thus we have $ \mathcal{C}^*= \mathcal{C}^*_{(n-1)/2} \bigcup \mathcal{C}^*_{(n+1)/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: C* splits over the two middle layers.

nodes.name: Bipartite layer graph
nodes.statement: For notation convenience, we set $n_1=(n-1)/2, n_2=(n+1)/2$. Let $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$ be the subgraph of $\widehat{G}$ induced by $\mathcal{C}_{n_1} \cup \mathcal{C}_{n_2}$. We can view $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$ as a bipartite graph with two disjoint vertex sets $\mathcal{C}_{n_1}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: View the two middle layers as a bipartite graph.

nodes.name: Edges from C*_{n1} avoid C*_{n2}
nodes.statement: Observe that $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1} \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{n_1}$ and $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2} \subseteq\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$. Let $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ be the set of edges induced by $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}$ in $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$. Since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$, none of the edges in $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ will have an end in a node of $\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}$, i.e, all the edges of $\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})$ should have an end falling in $\mathcal{C}_{n_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Independence forces edges from C*_{n1} into the complement of C*_{n2}.

nodes.name: Degree count
nodes.statement: Note that in $\widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}_{n_1}, \mathcal{C}_{n_2})$, all nodes have a degree of $n_2$. Thus we have: $$ |\widehat{E} (\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1})|=|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}|*n_2 \le |\mathcal{C}_{n_2} \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}|*n_2= (|\mathcal{C}_{n_2}|-|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}|)*n_2 $$ from which we obtain $|\mathcal{C}^*|=|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_1}|+|\mathcal{C}^*_{n_2}| \le |\mathcal{C}_{n_2}|$ $=$ ${n} \choose n_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Regularity gives |C*| <= C(n,n_2).

nodes.name: Bound attained
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathcal{C}_{n_2}$ itself is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$ with size $n \choose n_2$. Thus we conclude that $|\mathcal{C}^*|$ $=$ ${n} \choose n_2$ $= g(n)$.
nodes.statement_short: C_{n_2} attains the bound, so |C*| = g(n).

nodes.name: Assume L(n) small
nodes.statement: Let us assume $n$ is an even number. We prove by contradiction as follows. Suppose $L(n)=\ell \le n/2-1$.
nodes.statement_short: For even n, suppose L(n) = l <= n/2-1.

nodes.name: Construct C_new
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{C}^*_k \subseteq \mathcal{C}^*, L(n)\le k \le U(n)$ be the collection of all sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$ which has the size of $k$, i.e, $\mathcal{C}^*_k =\{S \in \mathcal{C}^*| |S|=k\}$. In the following we construct a new collection $\mathcal{C}_{new} \subseteq \mathcal{C} $ which proves to be an independent set in $\widehat{G}$ with the size being strictly larger than $\mathcal{C}^*$. For each $S \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$, we add to $\mathcal{C}^*$ all subsets of $V$ which has the form as $S\cup \{i\}$ where $i \in V \setminus S$ and remove $S$ from $\mathcal{C}^*$ meanwhile. Let $\mathcal{C}_{new} $ be the collection obtained after we process the same route for all $S \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$. Mathematically, we have: $\mathcal{C}_{new}= \mathcal{C}_1 \bigcup \mathcal{C}_2$ where $\mathcal{C}_1=\bigcup_{S\in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell } \bigcup_{i \in V \setminus S} \{ S\cup \{i\} \}, \mathcal{C}_2=\mathcal{C}^* \setminus \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$.
nodes.statement_short: Name the layers C*_k and replace each smallest set by all its one-element extensions.

nodes.name: C_new is independent
nodes.statement: First we show $\mathcal{C}_{new} $ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Arbitrarily choose two distinct sets, say $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_{new}, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_{new}, S_1 \ne S_2$. We check all the possible cases one by one: \begin{itemize} \item $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_1$. We observe that $|S_1|=|S_2|=\ell+1$ and $S_1 \ne S_2$. Thus no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$. \item $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_2, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_2$. In this case no inclusion relation can exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$ since $\mathcal{C}_2$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. \item $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_2$. Since $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell$ is the collection of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$ which has the smallest size $\ell$, we get that $|S_2| \ge \ell+1=|S_1|$. Therefore there is only one possible inclusion relation existing here, that is $S_1 \subset S_2$. Suppose $S_1= S_1^\prime \cup \{i_1\} \subset S_2 $ for some $S_1^\prime \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$. Thus we get that $S_1^\prime \subset S_2$ which implies $\mathcal{C}^*$ is not an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Hence we conclude that no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$. \end{itemize} Summarizing the analysis above, we get that no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$ which yields $\mathcal{C}_{new} $ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Show C_new is an independent set, by cases.

nodes.name: Pick two sets
nodes.statement: Arbitrarily choose two distinct sets, say $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_{new}, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_{new}, S_1 \ne S_2$. We check all the possible cases one by one:
nodes.statement_short: Take two distinct sets of C_new.

nodes.name: Both in C_1
nodes.statement: $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_1$. We observe that $|S_1|=|S_2|=\ell+1$ and $S_1 \ne S_2$. Thus no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal sizes: no inclusion.

nodes.name: Both in C_2
nodes.statement: $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_2, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_2$. In this case no inclusion relation can exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$ since $\mathcal{C}_2$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: C_2 is a subset of an independent set.

nodes.name: Mixed case
nodes.statement: $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}_1, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_2$. Since $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell$ is the collection of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$ which has the smallest size $\ell$, we get that $|S_2| \ge \ell+1=|S_1|$. Therefore there is only one possible inclusion relation existing here, that is $S_1 \subset S_2$. Suppose $S_1= S_1^\prime \cup \{i_1\} \subset S_2 $ for some $S_1^\prime \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$. Thus we get that $S_1^\prime \subset S_2$ which implies $\mathcal{C}^*$ is not an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Hence we conclude that no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$.
nodes.statement_short: An inclusion would contradict independence of C*.

nodes.name: Summarize
nodes.statement: Summarizing the analysis above, we get that no inclusion relation could exist between $S_1$ and $S_2$ which yields $\mathcal{C}_{new} $ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: So C_new is independent.

nodes.name: C_new is larger
nodes.statement: Now we prove that $|\mathcal{C}_{new} |>|\mathcal{C}^* | $. Observe that $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ are disjoint from each other; otherwise $\mathcal{C}^*$ is not an independent set. So we have $|\mathcal{C}_{new}|=|\mathcal{C}_1|+|\mathcal{C}_2|$. Note that $|\mathcal{C}^*|=|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|+|\mathcal{C}_2|$ since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is the union of the two disjoint parts $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$. Therefore $|\mathcal{C}_{new} |>|\mathcal{C}^* | $ is equivalent to $|\mathcal{C}_1 |>|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell | $. Let $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ be the induced subgraph graph of $\widehat{G}$ by $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell \bigcup \mathcal{C}_1$. Note that $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ can be viewed as a bipartite graph where the two disjoint vertex sets are $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell $ and $\mathcal{C}_1$ respectively. In $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ we observe that (1) for each node $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$, its degree $d(S_1)=n-\ell$; (2) for each node $S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_1$, its degree $d(S_2) \le \ell+1$. Thus we get that $ |\widetilde{E}|=|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell| (n-\ell) \le |\mathcal{C}_1|(\ell+1) $. According to our assumption we have $\ell \le n/2-1$. Thus we have \\ $|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|/|\mathcal{C}_1| \le (\ell+1)/ (n-\ell) \le (n/2)/(n/2+1)<1$, yielding $|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|< |\mathcal{C}_1|$ which is equivalent to $|\mathcal{C}^* | < |\mathcal{C}_{new} | $.
nodes.statement_short: Show |C_new| > |C*| by a bipartite degree count.

nodes.name: C_1 and C_2 disjoint
nodes.statement: Observe that $\mathcal{C}_1$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$ are disjoint from each other; otherwise $\mathcal{C}^*$ is not an independent set. So we have $|\mathcal{C}_{new}|=|\mathcal{C}_1|+|\mathcal{C}_2|$.
nodes.statement_short: C_1 and C_2 are disjoint.

nodes.name: Reduce to |C_1| > |C*_l|
nodes.statement: Note that $|\mathcal{C}^*|=|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|+|\mathcal{C}_2|$ since $\mathcal{C}^*$ is the union of the two disjoint parts $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell$ and $\mathcal{C}_2$. Therefore $|\mathcal{C}_{new} |>|\mathcal{C}^* | $ is equivalent to $|\mathcal{C}_1 |>|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell | $.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices that |C_1| > |C*_l|.

nodes.name: Bipartite subgraph
nodes.statement: Let $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ be the induced subgraph graph of $\widehat{G}$ by $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell \bigcup \mathcal{C}_1$. Note that $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ can be viewed as a bipartite graph where the two disjoint vertex sets are $\mathcal{C}^*_\ell $ and $\mathcal{C}_1$ respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Consider the bipartite graph between C*_l and C_1.

nodes.name: Degree count
nodes.statement: In $ \widehat{G}(\mathcal{C}^*_\ell, \mathcal{C}_1)$ we observe that (1) for each node $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*_\ell$, its degree $d(S_1)=n-\ell$; (2) for each node $S_2 \in \mathcal{C}_1$, its degree $d(S_2) \le \ell+1$. Thus we get that $ |\widetilde{E}|=|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell| (n-\ell) \le |\mathcal{C}_1|(\ell+1) $.
nodes.statement_short: Count edges: |C*_l|(n-l) <= |C_1|(l+1).

nodes.name: Ratio below one
nodes.statement: According to our assumption we have $\ell \le n/2-1$. Thus we have \\ $|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|/|\mathcal{C}_1| \le (\ell+1)/ (n-\ell) \le (n/2)/(n/2+1)<1$, yielding $|\mathcal{C}^*_\ell|< |\mathcal{C}_1|$ which is equivalent to $|\mathcal{C}^* | < |\mathcal{C}_{new} | $.
nodes.statement_short: With l <= n/2-1 the ratio is < 1.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: So far we have successfully constructed a new collection $\mathcal{C}_{new} \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ such that (1) it is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$ and (2) $ |\mathcal{C}_{new} |>|\mathcal{C}^* |$. That contradicts with the fact that $\mathcal{C}^*$ is a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Thus our assumption $\ell \le n/2-1$ does not hold, which yields $\ell \ge n/2$. For the case when $n$ is odd, we can process essentially the same analysis as above and get $\ell \ge (n-1)/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction with maximality of C*; odd n similar.

nodes.name: Dual collection
nodes.statement: Let us assume $n$ is an even number. Based on $\mathcal{C}^*$, we construct a dual collection $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ as follows: Initialize $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ as an empty collection. For each $S\in \mathcal{C}^*$, we add $V \setminus S$ into $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$. Mathematically, we have: $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}=\bigcup_{S\in \mathcal{C}^*} \{V \setminus S\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the complement collection of C*.

nodes.name: Dual is independent
nodes.statement: First we show $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. Arbitrarily choose two distinct sets, say $V \setminus S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*_{dual}, V \setminus S_2 \in \mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$, where $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}^*, S_1 \ne S_2$. Note that $$V \setminus S_1 \subset V \setminus S_2 \Leftrightarrow S_1 \supset S_2, V \setminus S_2 \subset V \setminus S_1 \Leftrightarrow S_2 \supset S_1 $$ Thus we have that no inclusion relation could exist between $V \setminus S_1$ and $V \setminus S_2$ since no inclusion relation exists between $S_1$ and $S_2$ resulting from the fact that $\mathcal{C}^*$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$. So we get $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ is an independent set as well.
nodes.statement_short: Complementation preserves non-inclusion.

nodes.name: Pick two sets
nodes.statement: Arbitrarily choose two distinct sets, say $V \setminus S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*_{dual}, V \setminus S_2 \in \mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$, where $S_1 \in \mathcal{C}^*, S_2 \in \mathcal{C}^*, S_1 \ne S_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Take two distinct complements.

nodes.name: Inclusion reverses
nodes.statement: Note that $$V \setminus S_1 \subset V \setminus S_2 \Leftrightarrow S_1 \supset S_2, V \setminus S_2 \subset V \setminus S_1 \Leftrightarrow S_2 \supset S_1 $$ Thus we have that no inclusion relation could exist between $V \setminus S_1$ and $V \setminus S_2$ since no inclusion relation exists between $S_1$ and $S_2$ resulting from the fact that $\mathcal{C}^*$ is an independent set of $\widehat{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion between complements reverses inclusion between sets.

nodes.name: Conclude independence
nodes.statement: So we get $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ is an independent set as well.
nodes.statement_short: The dual is independent.

nodes.name: Dual is largest
nodes.statement: We can verify that $|\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}|=|\mathcal{C}^*|$. Therefore we can conclude $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ is a largest independent set of $\widehat{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: Same size, so also a largest independent set.

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 4
nodes.statement: By Lemma~\ref{lem:Lowe-n}, we get to know the minimum size of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*_{dual}$ should be at least $n/2$, which yields the maximum size of of sets in $\mathcal{C}^*$ should be at most $n/2$. For the case when $n$ is odd, we can analyze essentially the same as above.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 4 on the dual bounds the maximum size in C*.

nodes.name: Split into two directions
nodes.statement: To prove the theorem we need to show the following. First, if $C$ is a clique emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:main}, then $C$ must be an $\alpha$-maximal clique. Next, if $C$ is an $\alpha$-maximal clique, then it will be emitted by Algorithm~\ref{algo:main}.
nodes.statement_short: Need soundness and completeness.

nodes.name: Apply Lemmas 8 and 9
nodes.statement: We prove them in Lemmas~\ref{lemma:correctness1}~and~\ref{lemma:correctness2} respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 8 and 9.

nodes.name: What to show
nodes.statement: Let $u' \in V$ be a vertex such that (1)~$u' > \max(C')$, and (2)~$C' \cup \{ u' \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. We need to show that $(u',r') \in I'$ such that $clq(C' \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot r'$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix a valid extension u' and show it is in I' with the right factor.

nodes.name: Call sequence
nodes.statement: Let $C'$ be a clique being called by Enum-Uncertain-MC with $I'$. Note that each call of the method adds one vertex $u \in I$ to the current clique $C$ such $u > \max(C)$. Since the vertices are added in the lexicographical ordering, there is an unique sequence of calls to the method Enum-Uncertain-MC such that we reach a point in execution of Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} where Enum-Uncertain-MC is called with $C'$. We call this sequence of calls as Call-$0$, Call-$1$, $\ldots$, Call-$\left | C' \right |$. Also, let $C_i$ be the clique used by method Enum-Uncertain-MC during Call-$i$.
nodes.statement_short: The unique sequence of calls reaching C'.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We prove by induction. First consider the base case. For that consider the first call made to Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs}, i.e. Call-$0$. We know that $C$ is initialized as $\emptyset$. During the first call made, all vertices in $V$ satisfy conditions (1) and (2). This is because, first $max(\emptyset) = 0$. Second any single vertex can be considered as a clique with probability $1$. $\hat{I}$ is initialized such that all $r$ in $\hat{I}$ are $1 \ge \alpha$. Thus for all u such that $(u,r) \in \hat{I}$, $u > \max(C)$. This proves the base case.
nodes.statement_short: Base: initial I-hat contains all vertices with factor 1.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: For the inductive step, consider a recursive call to the method Call-$i$ which calls Call-$(i+1)$. For every case expect initialization, $I'$ is generated from $I$ by line~\ref{algoline:genI} of Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} which in turn calls Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}. In Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}, only vertices in $I$ that are greater than $C'$ are added to $I'$. Thus all vertices in $I$ that satisfy (1) are added to $I'$. Next every vertex in $I$ is connected to $C$. We need to show that all vertices in $I'$ are connected to $C'$. In line 4 of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}, we prune out any vertex in $I$ that is not connected to $m = \max(C')$. Assume that $u'$ extends $C$ such that $clq(C \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = r$. Now let $c = \{ C' \setminus C$ \}. Note that $c$ is a single vertex. Also, assume $u' > c$. From line 4, we know that $q' \cdot r' \ge \alpha$ Also from line 6 of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI}, $r' = r \cdot p(\{c,u'\})$. Now $clq(C' \cup \{ u' \},\mathcal{G}) = q' \cdot r \cdot p(\{c,u'\}) = q' \cdot r'$, Now in line 8 of Algorithm~\ref{algo:generateI} we add $u'$ to $I'$ only if $r' \ge \alpha$ thus proving the inductive step.
nodes.statement_short: GenerateI keeps neighbours of the new vertex with updated factor r' = r p.

nodes.name: Parent call
nodes.statement: Let $m = \max(C')$ and $C = C' \setminus \{ m\}$. Since Algorithm~\ref{algo:dfs} was called with $C'$, it must have been called with $C$. This is because the working clique is always extended by adding vertices from $I$, and from Lemma~\ref{obs:I}, $I$ only contains vertices that are greater than the maximum vertex in $C$.
nodes.statement_short: The call with C' comes from a call with C = C' minus its max.

nodes.name: A valid smaller vertex
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be the corresponding set of tuples used when the call was made to Enum-Uncertain-MC with $C$. Let $u > \max(C)$ be a vertex such that $clq(C' \cup \{ u \},\mathcal{G}) \ge \alpha$ and $u < m$. Note that $u \not \in C'$, $u < \max(C')$, and $C' \cup \{ u \}$ is an $\alpha$-clique in $\mathcal{G}$. This means $u$ satisfies all conditions for $u \in X'$.
